title: Two souls
hook: the Tanya describes an animal soul and a godly soul in each person

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tanya, and its in-between person who feels the pull and still chooses. Your line was the in-between person. When an old pull showed up, did you name it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

The alarm goes off. One voice says: five more minutes, you've earned it. Another says: get up, there's someone you promised to call. You're hungry and someone at the table is hungrier. One voice says take the bigger piece. Another says pass it. An argument like that needs more than one voice in there. Yesterday's book, the Tanya, doesn't treat that as a glitch. It opens by giving the voices names. Today we meet them.
screen: `FIVE MORE MINUTES.` → `GET UP, YOU PROMISED.` → `MORE THAN ONE VOICE IN THERE.`

segments.voice: Two souls. The Tanya teaches that each Jew has two souls. First, the animal soul. It's the life of the body: hunger, tiredness, the instinct to protect yourself and get what you need. Animal here isn't an insult. Teachers of the Tanya explain it as the life a person shares with other living creatures. Its center is self: me first, mine, more. Second, the godly soul. The Tanya describes it with a phrase borrowed from the book of Job: a part of God above. Its pull is toward God, toward giving, toward the good beyond itself. Proverbs gives a picture that fits: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." Third, the city. In a later chapter the Tanya compares the body to a small city, and the two souls to two kings, each wanting to rule it. Every thought, every word, every act is a piece of ground one of them wins. That's yesterday's in-between person, seen from the inside: two kings, one city, and a daily choice about who governs. Fourth, the aim. The goal isn't to kill the animal soul. It keeps you alive. The hope, in Chabad teaching, is that the godly soul leads, and that over time even the animal soul's energy, its hunger and drive, can be turned toward good. Remember the lesson on serving through the body: the appetite isn't the enemy. It's the city's other citizen, waiting to be led well.
screen: `THE ANIMAL SOUL: THE LIFE OF THE BODY.` · `THE GODLY SOUL: A PART OF GOD ABOVE.` · `TWO KINGS, ONE SMALL CITY.` · `NOT TO KILL, BUT TO LEAD.` · then, large: `TWO SOULS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice both today, and begin now. Settle, and breathe. Listen inside for the animal soul. Maybe it's tired, or hungry, or wants this to be over. No need to argue with it. Just hear it: there you are. Now listen for the other voice, the one that leans toward someone else, toward the good, toward God if you pray. It may be quieter. That's all right. Hear it too: there you are. Sit with both for a while, two voices in one small city, and notice that you can hear each one. If you pray, you can ask that the quieter one lead. The bell holds the time.
Two souls. In the Tanya, the animal soul that gives life to the body, and the godly soul, a part of God above, each pulling toward its own. Today's word.
Your line: two souls. Today, at one decision, big or small, pause long enough to hear both voices before you choose. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: In Chabad study, the opening chapters of the Tanya on the animal soul and the godly soul are taught as a map of inner life, used to understand the struggle in prayer and in daily choices.

original.note: Hebrew: soul, life. The Tanya speaks of a nefesh of the animal and a nefesh of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good angel on one shoulder and a bad one on the other.
what it means: two souls in one person, the life of the body and a part of God above, each pulling toward its own.
what a scholar hears: the Tanya's opening chapters on the nefesh habahamit and the nefesh elokit, and its image of two kings and a small city.

notes: Proverbs 20:27 quoted from JPS 1917; please confirm.
The Tanya ch. 1 frames the two souls as belonging to each Jew; the script says 'each Jew' to stay true to the text. A Keeper may want to add how Chabad speaks of non-Jews' souls, or leave it.
'A part of God above' (chelek Eloah mima'al, Job 31:2, Tanya ch. 2) paraphrased.
'Called animal because it is the life a person shares with every creature' is a gloss; the Tanya's own account (the animal soul from kelipat nogah) is more technical. Confirm.
The two-kings-and-a-small-city image follows Tanya ch. 9, which draws on Ecclesiastes 9:14; confirm.
The angel/devil on the shoulder in the trapdoor is a popular image, not a claim about any tradition.
